subject: Agriculture
title: Can Organic Feed the World?
description: A micro-lesson that makes Can Organic Feed the World? usable.

hook.text: If all farming went organic tomorrow, would the world starve? The answer depends entirely on what else changes.

buildup.text: Pure yield comparison says no—organic produces 20% less. We'd need 20% more farmland or feed 20% fewer people.

discovery.text: But 30% of food is wasted. 36% of grain feeds animals, not humans. The system, not just the yield, is the problem.

twist.text: A 2017 study found 100% organic is feasible if food waste drops 50% and animal feed from cropland drops by a third.

climax.text: The question isn't 'can organic feed the world?' It's 'can organic feed the world we're willing to build?'

punchline.text: Organic can feed everyone—if we change what 'everyone eats' looks like.

quiz.question: Under what conditions could 100% organic farming feed the world?
options: If food waste drops 50% and feed crop use is reduced

details.summary: Whether organic agriculture can scale to feed the global population is one of the most debated questions in food policy. This topic examines yield comparisons, land use implications, food waste reduction, and the role of dietary change in making organic viable at scale.
details.whyItMatters: Answering this question shapes agricultural policy for billions of people. The answer depends not just on yields but on food waste, diet composition, and how we measure agricultural success beyond simple output.
takeaways: Studies suggest organic could feed the world if food waste is halved and diets shift
The answer depends on assumptions about land use, diets, and waste reduction
A hybrid approach combining organic principles with targeted technology is most likely

faq.question: What does research say about organic agriculture's ability to feed the world?
faq.answer: A major 2017 study in Nature Communications found organic agriculture could feed 9 billion people if combined with reduced food waste and less livestock feed from cropland. The yield gap is real but can be offset by systemic changes in food distribution and consumption.

faq.question: Why do experts disagree on whether organic can scale globally?
faq.answer: Disagreement centers on assumptions. Optimists include reduced waste, dietary shifts, and improved organic practices. Skeptics focus on current yield gaps and the additional land needed. Both sides agree that neither pure organic nor pure conventional is the optimal path.
